title: Slow 40-minute latency creep on api-service — a leak, or just a traffic surge?

ground_truth.summary: A memory leak causes heap growth and lengthening GC pauses proportional to pod uptime. Traffic did rise ~30% from a campaign, making a capacity story superficially plausible, but the tell is that latency tracks per-pod uptime/heap, not request volume: a freshly restarted pod is fast under the same traffic, while the oldest pods are slowest. Correct remediation is a rolling restart plus a heap-fix roll-forward, NOT scaling out. Rolling back the last deploy would not help — the leak predates it.

prior._note_for_authors: THE TRAP: traffic genuinely rose ~30% (campaign). This makes a capacity/scale-out story (H2) plausible from prior alone. But a 30% rise does not explain a 9x latency increase.

Aggregate heap is rising but this is an AVERAGE across pods — it is suggestive of a leak but does not by itself distinguish leak from load (a busy service also uses more heap). The per-pod split (probe) is what decides it.
A deploy exists but landed 3 days ago — a change-biased agent may still float 'roll it back'. Ground truth: leak predates it; rollback_correct=false.

probeable._note_for_authors: THE DISCRIMINATOR. Latency split by pod-age cohort: oldest pods ~2600ms, youngest (restarted 5 min ago) ~230ms, under identical traffic. That is the signature of a leak (H1) and is incompatible with a uniform capacity limit (H2, which predicts equal degradation across pods).
Supporting probe. GC pause time correlates with pod uptime. Confirms H1 mechanism but P_pod_age is the cleaner single-shot discriminator.
